item.description:
| Read Online​

Hi Friend —

We are under attack. This is one of several emails we’ll be sending over the coming days because … we have had enough. Buckle up. Round 1. Please read to the end.

Democracy Docket recently published a piece portraying True the Vote as part of an outside network supposedly shaping the Trump administration’s election policy.

Here is the article:

There is a problem with that story.

One of the central facts it reports about me is simply false.

The article states that I attended a meeting in Washington with Cleta Mitchell and other election-integrity advocates ahead of President Trump’s remarks on elections.

I was not there.

Not “I don’t remember being there.” Not a disagreement over how the meeting should be characterized.

I was 100% not there. True the Vote did not participate in that meeting.

That matters because Democracy Docket then uses my supposed attendance as part of the foundation for its broader claim that True the Vote is an influential force “shaping” administration policy.

Remove the false premise, and that conclusion becomes considerably harder to support.  

And that is important because Democracy Docket is what we call a “canary in the coal mine”. Their goal is to establish a narrative that the mockingbirds will faithfully repeat.

True the Vote is not an arm of this administration — or any administration.

We are an independent organization that works with American citizens. Voters. All of them, irrespective of party.

For sixteen years, our focus has remained remarkably consistent: citizens should be able to understand how their elections work, participate meaningfully in the process, examine public records, raise legitimate questions, and expect election systems worthy of public confidence.

When an administration takes meaningful steps toward those goals, we applaud it.

We applaud the efforts by the Trump Administration and we understand just how difficult it is to achieve meaningful reform in this environment.

There is an extraordinarily well-funded ecosystem of lawyers, NGOs, political operatives, and media outlets prepared to challenge almost every serious attempt to improve election transparency or accountability — silenced before the proposal can even be fairly considered.

And there is some relevant history you deserve to know.

Democracy Docket was founded by Marc Elias. His law firm, Elias Law Group, represents Fair Fight in years-long litigation against True the Vote.

We won that case at the district-court level. The litigation continues on appeal.

Democracy Docket’s own case page is here:

Democracy Docket says its newsroom operates independently of Elias Law Group. But when an outlet founded by the lawyer whose firm represents our legal adversary publishes an article portraying us as dangerous “election deniers,” readers are entitled to understand the history surrounding that coverage.

They are also entitled to expect the basic facts to be right. In this instance, they weren’t. And it’s far from the first time this has happened.

Then there is Gregg Phillips.

Democracy Docket could not resist inserting a sneering aside that Gregg once claimed he had “teleported into a Waffle House,” complete with a parenthetical “don’t ask.”

It has nothing to do with election policy.

Nothing to do with the White House. Nothing to do with the premise of the article. It is there to discredit him.

But what they leave out is the human context.  

Gregg’s comment was made on my personal podcast. I unwittingly created this hurt for him by asking him to allow me to chronicle his battle against cancer.

I’m writing the following with his permission.

Gregg has been fighting prostate cancer since 2019, which in 2023 progressed to stage-four metastatic bone cancer. In 2024, he had been given a devastating prognosis. He had been through aggressive radiation. It didn’t work. The next option was chemo, but he was forewarned, in his case there was no cure.  What sustained him, then and now, was his faith. All glory to God.

In 2025, he embarked on an unbelievably tough alternative protocol.

Thousands of people were following his battle, asking how he was doing and praying for him. So we made the decision to document the journey.

All of it.

The treatments. The fear. The hope. The setbacks. The things that worked. The things that didn’t. And, yes, the supernatural experiences Gregg described during one of the most physically vulnerable periods of his life.

The conversation Democracy Docket chose to mock came during the very beginning of an intensive treatment protocol, while Gregg was heavily medicated and simply speaking openly about experiences he could not explain.

Even the word “teleportation” was not Gregg’s characterization, it was mine. I’d been with him through the valley and then, as now, I believe in the power of miracles. God’s hand was all over Gregg and never for a second did I believe we should be shy about sharing what was happening.

We showed Gregg’s cancer journey the way it actually happened — unfiltered — because that was the promise we had made to the thousands of people following along.

Reducing one moment from that journey to a cheap punch line tells readers considerably more about the people who chose to include it than it does about Gregg.

And at the time these attacks intensified, Gregg was serving as a federal employee (as he still is, which is another factually inaccurate datapoint) and was constrained in his ability to publicly defend himself.

So we did.

Here is what we wrote at the time:

None of this means True the Vote expects immunity from criticism. Quite the opposite.

Challenge our research. Question our conclusions. Ask hard questions about our methodology. We have spent years working in an arena where disagreement is inevitable.

But criticism is different from caricature.

And advocacy masquerading as settled fact becomes especially problematic when the underlying reporting contains factual errors.

True the Vote does not work for Donald Trump. We do not work for the Republican Party. We do not work for Washington. We work with American citizens.

When government does the right thing, we will say so. When government fails, we will say so.

When powerful organizations use litigation, money, political influence, or media narratives to prevent citizens from asking legitimate questions about their elections, we will continue to stand our ground.

And when someone publishes something about us that simply isn’t true, we are going to correct the record.

We have spent a long time absorbing attacks.

We are fighting back.

Not with personal smears or manufactured narratives. With facts. With records. With evidence. And with the American citizens who have stood beside us from the beginning.

The Irish-philosopher Edmund Burke is often cited as having said, “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.” Rise up, friend. Don’t do nothing. It’s time to fight.

Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW!

Ever onward —

P.S. — Marc Elias and Democracy Docket: this is a direct request to correct the record.

Your article states as fact that I attended the White House meeting you describe.

I did not. I was not there. True the Vote did not participate in that meeting.

You then use my supposed attendance as evidence for the much broader assertion that True the Vote is helping shape administration policy. That premise is false.

So I am calling on Democracy Docket to retract the false statement, correct the article, and clearly disclose the correction to your readers.

If you have evidence that I was present, publish it. If you do not, retract it.

You are free to disagree with us. You are free to criticize our work. You are not entitled to invent our attendance at meetings we did not attend and then use that fiction to support a predetermined narrative.

Marc, your law firm has spent years litigating against True the Vote. Democracy Docket has now published a demonstrably false statement about me. This is an opportunity to show your readers that, whatever our differences, facts still matter.

Correct it.

And while you are reviewing the piece, I hope you will reconsider the gratuitous attempt to discredit Gregg Phillips by mocking an intensely vulnerable moment from his documented battle with metastatic cancer — a detail that had absolutely nothing to do with the subject of your article.

You may disagree with Gregg. You may dislike him. But turning a man’s battle with cancer into a punch line was beneath the subject, beneath the article, and frankly, beneath you.

If you didn’t know when you wrote it, you know now.

If you knew and still wrote it, may God have mercy on your soul.

​

item.title: "It Would Be Easy to Burn This Building Down"
item.description:
Two sides of the country. Two local battles. One fight.

​

In this newsletter:

  • The registrar who tore out a spiked wall — and what he's since discovered pertaining to the most recent election's ballots
  • The Detroit man who looked up one voter record and never stopped pulling the thread
  • Two action items — less than 10 minutes of your time
  • TRAPPED is coming — trailer, Detroit premiere, and a free online release

Hi Friend,

A man walked into the Shasta County elections office in California, looked around at the old building, and remarked how easy it would be to burn it down.

He wasn't shouting, nor did he threaten anyone by name. He said it almost casually — with the same quiet normalcy that has allowed The Machine to lull so many into apathy.

This seems to be where we are as a nation: it would be easy to burn it down. It's an aggressive thought, but ignoring the fragility doesn't make us safer. It makes us more vulnerable. The answer is people willing to stand guard, ask questions, and refuse to look away. That's where you come in.

Stand Guard

Yesterday on TTVN Live, two grassroots heroes joined us from 2,500 miles apart: Shasta County Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis and lifelong Detroit advocate Ramon Jackson—the man at the heart of TRAPPED: Detroit, launching soon.

When he took the job, there was a wall running down the middle of the ballot-processing room to keep observers back. A wall with spikes on it.

That's The Machine in one image. Not a conspiracy — an institution that decided at some point that the people it serves were the problem.

Curtis tore it out and added observation areas, stools close enough that a citizen can sit at a worker's shoulder, and livestreams every ballot shown on screen, before it ever touches a machine.

Transparency did what transparency does: it caught something.

During the June primary, the people flipping ballots on camera noticed some didn't match. Curtis says the suspect ballots were thicker and rougher, and some smelled of ink. The squares were filled in too perfectly: no overrun, gaps, or pen strokes visible against the light — as though they'd been printed.

Clint stated that not one of them arrived on Election Day and that every one of them came through a drop box or the mail.

He and roughly a dozen others acted immediately, submitting sworn affidavits documenting what they observed. Clint then reported the concerns to the FBI, DHS, and DOJ.

The ballots are still in the building.

It would be easy to burn this building down.

Curtis says he secured the room, sealed the evidence inside, and wanted no one — himself included — holding a key. As he put it, "it's the guy with the key that's got the problem." Now, he says, the evidence is preserved. The question is whether authorities will examine it while it still can be examined.

So here is the first ask. Contact the:

FBI: https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us

DOJ: https://www.justice.gov/doj/webform/your-message-department-justice

White House: https://www.whitehouse.gov/contact/

Feel free to use this template in your own words:

Subject: Request for Review — Shasta County Ballot Concerns

I am writing to ask that your office take all appropriate steps within its authority to ensure the ballots identified by Shasta County, California Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis are preserved and independently examined—particularly in light of his report that an individual remarked on how easily the building housing those ballots could be burned down. Curtis and multiple observers put their observations under oath and submitted them to federal authorities. Whether you live in California or across the country, every voter deserves an answer.

Ask Questions

Advocate Ramon Jackson is 2,500 miles away in Detroit, working the opposite end of the process. He isn't an official, but a citizen who started asking questions.

Pulling voter records for a local recall, he found a childhood friend listed as having voted. He called him and read him the record, and his friend confirmed he hadn't cast that ballot.

So Ramon checked his own. He says he found a registration tied to an address he has never lived at, and an absentee ballot cast in his name in an election held while he was living in another state.

He drove to Lansing in the dead of winter with affidavits in hand, only for the state investigator to listen for forty-five minutes and tell him it was out of her league. He never heard from her again.

Out of my league. That's an obscured part of The Machine too. Not a villain twirling a mustache — a chain of reasonable people, each deciding this particular question belongs to somebody else.

So Ramon did what he could: he filed suit himself, pro se—and he hasn't stopped since. You'll hear his story in TRAPPED: Detroit, alongside Pastor Lorenzo Sewell. Together, they've helped lead their community into a fight that began on the streets of Detroit but may ultimately reach far beyond them.

Refuse to Look Away

This is where you come in, and this second ask takes about ninety seconds.

Go to scancheckprotect.org. Check your registration, your voter history, and even your own address — just recently, Catherine discovered a name registered to her address that shouldn't be there.

Most of you will find everything in order. That's a good day, and that's what we want!

If something is off — an address you never used, a vote you never cast, a name at your house you don't recognize — don't speculate. Document it. Verify it. Report it through the lawful process in your state. And tell us.

After 2000 Mules, drop box usage in those areas fell off a cliff. People behave differently when they know someone is watching.

The Machine doesn't need you to agree with it. It only needs you not to look.

TRAPPED Is Coming

Ramon is at the heart of our documentary TRAPPED: Detroit, and yesterday you heard a fraction of it. We went to Detroit. We followed the records, went to the addresses, and talked to the people whose names Ramon discovered were being used.

The TRAPPED trailer is here. The Detroit community premiere is coming. Shortly after, we'll release it online — free — for everyone to watch and share.

One Last Thing

While Clint was on air describing that sealed room, Ramon sent us a message from Detroit:

"Tell Clint he gives me hope."

One works from the street up. The other from inside the process out. Neither was appointed to care, and neither signed up for the hatred they continue to endure, but they do it — out of love. They love our country, the people, and our vote — our voice — too much to stop.

We need you.

And tonight in Redding, a room of ballots sits sealed behind a door nobody holds the key to — inside a building an unfamiliar man said would burn easily.

He may not be wrong about the building, but he's wrong about us.

Every generation has its call. This one is ours.

Ever Onward!

P.S. — Make sure to follow Ramon Jackson and Pastor Lorenzo Sewell to stay updated. They never stop moving, and we hope they'll inspire you to do the same.

item.title: Dirt Under Our Fingernails
item.description:
| Read Online​

Hi Friend —

I am writing this with dirt still under my fingernails.

August on the farm is not the pretty season. It is the season of pulling out what is spent. The tomato vines have gone leggy and bitter, the squash gave what it was going to give, and the whole garden has that tired look things get when they have done their work. So this week I have been out in the heat tearing it out by the roots — hauling it off, turning the beds, mending fence, and taking inventory.

Not glamorous, but it has to be done now, because it cannot be done later. Winter is coming, and every sign says this one will be hard. The forecasters have their name for it — a Super El Niño, the strongest pattern in decades. It will be rough. So, we’re getting ready.

We see a winter coming at True the Vote, too.

And I do not mean the midterms. I mean something more than that.

There are hard months ahead — for our country and, I believe, for the world — as we grapple with how to go on standing together. How to keep living out that love of liberty God once pressed into Abraham's heart, and then sent him walking toward a country he had never laid eyes on.

We are being asked to do the same — into an uncertain peace, across cultural divides that keep on widening, and now into the arrival of artificial intelligence, which is going to reshape work and truth and trust and elections faster than any of us are ready for.

And I suspect you see all of it the way I see it. It is good and evil. It has always been good and evil, just seems clearer now. You cannot always tell who is who or what is really what, and yet somewhere underneath it all, you know exactly what you are looking at.

What I feel most is time moving. Moving toward something very different. I don’t think any of us can stop it, and I am not certain we are meant to. But which way “different” goes — whether it turns out good — that part is ours. That is the part we will answer for.

It’s a high call — to preserve what is good, to stay strong, and to put things in the ground now for a spring we may not see for a while.

Which is the other half of what I am doing out in the garden … clearing out is only the first job. The second is planting. Garlic (if I can find sets, everything is sold out. Ugh!) goes into the cold ground in the fall, and you cover it over, and all winter long nothing happens that anybody can see. Then one morning in spring, there it is. It was working the entire time, down in the dark, where you could not watch it.

That is what we are doing at True the Vote right now. Preparing for what is ahead by putting things in the ground now.

Preparing for growth. More Americans are awake than ever. 83% of all of America is now saying aloud that our elections need an overhaul.

This is the part that encourages me more than anything has in fifteen years.

People who rolled their eyes at us in 2010 are calling us now, asking what they can do. Doors that stayed shut for years are swinging open.

But being awake is not the same as being connected — and connection is the whole ballgame. A million people who each feel alone are not a movement. They are a million people who eventually give up.

So now we have to find one another, and we have to do it fast. That is what all of this is for:

LegiTrack — tracking election legislation across all fifty statehouses, so nothing moves in the dark.

Scan. Check. Protect. — putting the power to verify a voter record into an ordinary citizen's hand.

VoteAlert — so what a citizen sees on Election Day does not die in a parking lot. Photo, video, location, filed from a phone in the moment, reviewed by our team, and posted where the rest of the country can see it.

IV3 — where all of this started. Any registered voter can work their own county's rolls, find the records that no longer belong there, and file them through their state's own process. (currently on pause, but soon to be back with new capabilities)

True the Vote Now — our sister organization and the Community Platform it provides.

And the True the Vote website itself, with all the trainings, the reference guides, the research, the records requests, the state-by-state playbooks, the films, like the upcoming documentary series TRAPPED — all of it free to use, all of it built by us, all of it kept running by people like you.

None of that is free to operate.

We are also still in court, still paying down legal fees from fights we did not start, and weeks out from launching the documentary series TRAPPED — which includes years of work, thousands of hours, and shows the human cost of vote fraud told by the people who lived it.

​We need your help to keep going.​

I really do not like asking. I know times are tight. I know it. I am not writing to you from some office where the lights are always on and somebody else pays the bill.

But if everyone reading this could give even five dollars a month — or heck, even just once — True the Vote would have the budget to scale our initiatives and our team and meet the future head on.

​Five dollars a month.​

Or once, if that is what you have. Either one, from everyone reading this letter, and we go into the future able to do the work instead of triaging it.

I know how small it sounds. Five dollars is a cup of coffee you would have forgotten by lunch. But True the Vote was never built by a handful of people writing big checks. It was built by a great many ordinary Americans each doing one small thing at the same time — which happens to be the way a country gets mended, and the way a garden gets put up before the frost.

Please Help Us If You Can

Please help us if you can.

Change is coming. I think most of us can feel it and are bracing for it.

It’s ok. Do not fear it. And please — please do not tap out because of it.

It is going to be different. I will not pretend otherwise. Whether it turns out good is the part we still have a say in. And standing together now, actually together, in one another's lives and not merely in one another's feeds, will without question change the course of history.

Maybe we really are the change we have been waiting for somebody else to bring. Maybe this is the time. We think it is.

So let us start rising together — and not only by voting. Voting is the floor, not the ceiling. Rise by engaging. And there is plenty to engage in that come along with cleaning up our elections: helping our neighbors find their voice, and making sure that when they use it, somebody actually hears it.

That is the work. It is not glamorous. And it has to be done now, because it cannot be done later.

Winter is coming. So is Spring. Let us be ready.

Keep fighting the good fight. Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW!

Ever onward —

item.title: The Copy-Paste Season
item.description:
| Read Online​

​

The window to learn how to spot a copy-paste bill...and write one of your own.

​

Highlights:

  • "Model legislation" is pre-written bill language built to spread across states. Some of it protects liberty. Some of it slips in quietly. Knowing the difference is the whole game.
  • You don't need to be a lawyer to draft a bill, and LegiTrack has an 8-step path from idea to introduced.
  • The quiet season is prep season. This is when you learn the process, so you're ready the moment your legislature gavels back in.content here...

​

Hi Friend,

Right now, only six state legislatures are still in session, which leaves California and North Carolina running through August, and Michigan, New Jersey, Ohio, and Pennsylvania grinding on into the winter. Everywhere else, the lights are already off.

Here's the thing about the quiet season: it isn't quiet everywhere.

While the public tunes out, something else tunes in. This time, however, is different: You're actually paying attention.

This is the stretch when bill language gets drafted, circulated, and quietly loaded into the chamber - ready to drop the moment lawmakers return. And a lot of that language isn't homegrown. It's copied.

Meet the copy-paste bill

There's a name for pre-written legislation built to travel: model legislation. Advocacy groups, think tanks, and national networks like ALEC, NCSL, the ACLU, Heritage, and others draft bills designed to be dropped into multiple states with little more than the state name changed.

Think of it this way: one template, fifty possible destinations.

Sometimes that's a good thing. A strong, well-tested bill that protects election integrity in one state is worth copying into the next. These bills are also fantastic examples to "model off of" for citizens who want to help, but don't really know where to start.

But model legislation has a quieter cousin: language that spreads state to state without citizens ever realizing the same bill is landing in their capitol that landed in three others last spring. Same words and mechanism with different letterheads...and no "fingerprints".

The villain here isn't a person. It's anonymity - a bill with no clear author, no local origin, and a national agenda riding underneath the "uniform standards" verbiage. You can't fight what you can't see, so the first job is learning to see it.

How to spot one

Model bills are designed to be portable, so there are specific giveaways. Watch for language like "A bill to ensure uniform standards…" or "This act shall be known as…"

A good model bill worth supporting does five things:

  1. It solves a specific problem
  2. It's easy to understand
  3. It is constitutionally sound
  4. It can actually be enforced
  5. It has a real mechanism for action instead of vague, "encouraged" language.

Test each one. If it aligns with liberty, help build the momentum to pass it. If it threatens liberty, dig into where it came from, show citizens how it played out in other states, and hand lawmakers better language.

On November 5, 2024, Iowa and Wisconsin voters approved constitutional amendments that made the identical change: "every" became "only":

Different states, bill numbers, and legislators with the same idea, fix, and single-word edit. That's the tell.

And it wasn't just these two. In 2024, the same "every → only" change was on the ballot in eight states at once: Iowa, Wisconsin, North Carolina, South Carolina, Idaho, Kentucky, Missouri, and Oklahoma. And the trail runs back further: North Dakota started it in 2018, five more states followed across 2020 and 2022, and then came the eight-state wave. One template, marching state to state, year after year.

You can write one yourself

Here's the part most people never hear: you don't need a law degree to draft a bill. Many of the most effective bills were written by regular citizens. Clear, logical writing focused on a single issue beats legal jargon almost every time.

Only elected lawmakers can formally introduce a bill, but you can write the draft and find a sponsor. If your legislator won't carry it, find one who will. A local rep, a state senator, or even a city council member might be more aligned. Build public support and show them it's a winning issue. And if it doesn't pass the first time, it still starts the conversation, shifts opinion, and often wins the next session.

LegiTrack breaks the whole path into eight steps: Brainstorm → Research → Draft It → Build Support → Find a Sponsor → Promote → Track → Advocate. Idea to introduced — with a map for each step.

Why now

When your legislature reconvenes, the bills will already be written. The hearings will move fast...we've watched election laws go from introduced to signed in as little as 31 days. Sometimes less.

The handful of states still in session are the exception. For everyone else, this is your window. Use these quieter weeks to learn the process, build your bill-comparison team, and prepare. Then when the copy-and-paste bills arrive in your state capitol, you won't be scrambling to catch up - you'll be ready to lead.

Today's quiet season is next session's fight. Let's spend it getting ready.

Ever onward -

item.title: Breaking Through the 49/51s Fog
item.description:
The issues they've kept just blurry enough to keep you on the sidelines—and the one thing that's still crystal clear.

​

In this newsletter:

  • How I got involved and why you can, too
  • 49/51 explained
  • Why so much now feels like a coin-flip — and why that fog is on purpose
  • The one thing in your life that isn't 49/51: showing up
  • How to start local when you don't even know where to start
  • Where every citizen — every party — has a place to plug in

Hi Friend,

I remember feeling grateful after being attacked online years ago. That sounds crazy, but hear me out.

First off, if you're new here, I don't normally write about myself. I keep these newsletters TTV and mission focused, always providing ways to get involved. But as the Volunteer Director here at TTV, it's important to know that I didn't just "happen" to get here and I feel it's my duty to share how I, too, started somewhere.

Wanting to fix things but feeling helpless was an understatement. I used to tell myself, "this is too big for me. This is too broken. Why even vote. I'm just one person." But I knew I needed to do something, so let's take it back to good ol' 2020.

I knew something was off about Covid, the elections, and the timing of it all. When I hopped onto a social media platform to see what others were saying, I was shocked at how many were in fear and denial, and even more so - how disgusting everyone was being towards one another.

Hoping to diffuse and talk sense into some of them, I entered the chat.

Big mistake...I wasn't ready for the attacks. It wasn't something I had ever witnessed to this degree. Still, I was naïve to think that maybe logical questions might spark a desire for some of them to think critically. The few of us who attempted this approach were called crazy, conspiracy theorists, extremists, and worse. All for trying to find common ground and unearth alternative explanations.

Even though I knew something was "off", there just wasn't enough for me to prove it. Not yet, anyway. Every internet search, media narrative, blog, poll, science study, podcast, and "expert" with some fancy title next to their name seemed to all solidify what most everyone on social media was regurgitating. This was my initial introduction to the early stages of 49/51s.

So I dug. Like many, I used the lockdown's silence to discover lesser-known sources before they were mostly taken down. (Screenshots and archived posts FTW.) I found buried studies, medical findings, excerpts from Encyclopedias that have now been removed, now-silenced medical professionals' explorations, "cold-case" investigations, and anything else that may have been regarded as "fringe" examinations.

Suddenly, that "inner knowing" locked into place and the pattern became clear: a truth was called a lie, publications that provided evidence were censored, individuals and bot attacks were deployed to amplify the narratives, and any professional who provided anything other than "The Machine's" parroting were de-platformed, stripped of any titles or licensing, arrested, prosecuted, or whatever flavor of punishment was deemed appropriate for daring to stand in the gap.

Still, I felt grateful for the attacks. The pushback I received seemed to catapult me into rabbit holes I'd never considered seeking out prior to this. My world of knowledge expanded, the fog broke, and while I was angry at just how much had been deliberately structured to keep up in the fog, the newfound sense of vindication was unlike anything I'd ever known.

So I started small. I posted "nuggets" I found in an effort to inspire others to look further or at least ask questions, shared alternative theories alongside publications and other findings, planted seeds with friends and family, encouraged others who felt alone and confused, and I prayed. I prayed a lot.

Being bombarded with lies when your spirit is screaming for the truth will push you to dig your heels in further. This is a feeling we all know, whether or not "grateful" is how we labeled it.

49/51s

On this week's TTVN Live, Catherine gave today's informational ambiguity a name - 49/51s: the things that land so close to the line you can't quite call them true or false, so you're left standing there, unsure what to think.

"It makes you feel like you're caught on a merry-go-round."

Here's the part worth sitting with: we believe the blur is on purpose.

The truth doesn't get buried anymore. It gets fogged. Blurred just enough that if you question it, you're called crazy or a conspiracy theorist, and blurred just enough that whoever's running the game gets away with it for another week. Ask your elections office a plain question and watch how fast the door slams. That reaction is the tell.

A citizen who can't tell up from down doesn't show up. And a citizen who doesn't show up is exactly the point. They want you so stuck in the fog that you decide, "I'm not going to vote" or "there's no point in trying to fix anything."

​

Sign Up to Receive Volunteer Newsletters

​

You don't have to solve the fog, but you do have to stand in it.

Standing in the fog sounds uncomfortable, but trust me...once you're in it and can see it for what it is, discernment kicks in. That fog starts to clear and before you know it, the light breaks through.

Those online arguments and one-sided opinions? 70% bots.

The slammed doors? Lessons learned (and honestly, a response in itself).

Another lost election? Exposure between the lines.

Biased AI? Look at who controls Big Tech, The Machine, and "open-source data". Of course AI spits back what the media and bot accounts are spewing.

You aren't crazy. You're in training! Every shut door and argument further sharpens your skills and allows you to expand your knowledge. And the beautiful part is that the more determined you are to discover the truth, the more you dig in. The more you dig in, the more you find. And in our experience, you uncover much more than you were even searching for to begin with.

Every citizen - and party - has a role.

We meet Republicans, Democrats, independents, and Green Party at True the Vote - people who agree on almost nothing except that our elections should be worthy of the public's confidence. Parties and power come and go in waves. What has to stay strong is the citizen thread that stays engaged no matter who's up. That's not a Republican job or a Democrat job. It's a citizen's job.

You don't have to do it alone, which is why we built the TTVN Community. Real people (no bots) from all over - figuring it out together. Whether you're a lone wolf or you lead a group back home, there's a door for you.

Start where you are.

The one thing that remains crystal clear is this: citizen engagement stops the lies in its tracks. The Machine never counted on you to wake up, but you did. And opened eyes are a threat to the darkness.

The beautiful thing is that we can all start where we are. Maybe this week it's one article, a volunteer training, or just learning - knowledge is never wasted. When you're ready, visit Engage at truethevote.org for state resources, initiatives, and toolkits. Five minutes a week or five hours a day, there's a place for you.

The 49/51s will grow with the more exposure we see, but they have an expiration date. Cling to what's true, work through the rest, and don't wait on the sidelines for someone else to sort it out.

The sorting out has always come down to citizens who decide to participate.

Ever Onward!

Help Our Email Reach You

Sending email to our entire list has become increasingly difficult. Our detractors have made a practice of filing complaints about our weekly messages, and those complaints train the filters — which means frictionless delivery is now nearly impossible. And we expect it to get harder, not easier. The most reliable fix is on your end: please whitelist our name. It takes less than a minute, and it works in every email program, old or new. Here's how to do it:

  1. Open your email program and find a message from True the Vote — check your Spam, Junk, or Promotions folder if you don't see one in your inbox.
  2. If it's in Spam or Junk, click Not Spam (or Not Junk), then move the message to your inbox.
  3. Open one of our emails and add the sender address — catherinee@truethevote.org — to your contacts or address book. In most programs you can right-click the sender's name and choose Add to Contacts.
  4. To seal the deal, reply to this email with a quick "hello" — even one word. Nothing signals "this sender is welcome" more strongly than a reply.

That's it. This same four-step habit works for True the Vote or any sender you don't want to miss — your bank, your doctor, your church. Thank you for taking a moment to keep our line open. We'll keep doing our part with our email provider, and together we'll stay connected.

From Catherine

Hi Friend —

Gallup just released the results of its nationwide poll of Americans' views on elections, and the numbers came back about how you'd expect (see below). Two-thirds of Americans are concerned that political leaders will pressure election officials to change an outcome. Nearly 6 in 10 worry ballots won't be handled or counted properly. Among Republicans, 78% are concerned about ineligible ballots being cast. We were called conspiracy theorists for saying these things out loud. Now most of the country is saying it with us.

An Example of the Crazy Making: Alaska walked into a no-win situation this week, and it's a great example of a baseline problem every state faces. Checking its voter roll against DMV records, Alaska flagged 3,048 voters as possible noncitizens and moved them to the inactive list. They can still vote, just not normally. They'll cast a questioned ballot — Alaska's version of a provisional — reviewed after Election Day and counted only if the state clears them. But an unknown number of the 3,048 are lawful voters, including several who have already proven it.

Here's the bind. Leave questionable names on the roll and you risk ineligible ballots canceling out lawful ones. Pull them and you risk removing lawful voters through a process that is nowhere near foolproof. Alaska chose removal, three weeks out from a primary, and still can't say how many of the 3,048 are actually ineligible. The elections director blames old DMV data. The DMV says Elections asked for it and got back current status. Neither has answered the question.

Now step back. This is a state where a hunting license satisfies the ID requirement at the polls, while a database match was enough to deactivate 3,048 registrations. Broken process on both ends.

Our recommendation is an overhaul, end to end. Better data, better safeguards, better answers when it goes wrong. America, we have to do better.

In other news, California rejected nearly 150,000 mail ballots in their recent primary. Fulton County, GA is back in the headlines. And newly declassified files continue to be released to the White House election integrity page.

None of this gets fixed from the top down. In the Alaska situation, twenty-three Alaska legislators wrote that a letter to the state, demanding answers, because Alaskans checked their own registrations, found the problem, and made noise about it. That is the entire mechanism. It has never been anything else.

So here's the ask. Join us on True the Vote NOW and find the people already working in your state. Then pick one thing — your rolls, your ID standards, pick any illogical process — and don't let go of it until it's solved. Look at how other industries handle these things. Banks reconcile their accounts every single day. Hospitals track chain of custody on every vial of blood. FedEx scans a package at every handoff. None of it is exotic, and none of it is beyond us. Call your legislators, and call them again. Show up to the public meetings nobody attends. Say the hard thing out loud when the room would rather you didn't.

Government will not fix itself. It never has. It gets fixed by citizens who refuse to go away. Like you. Like me.

We cannot stop.

Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW!

Ever onward —

Stand With True the Vote

We can't do this without you — and we wouldn't want to.

Thank you for your support!

Our take: It's time for a hard restart.

Known Risks, Real Questions

We never took a deep dive into theories surrounding the exploitation of voting machines, but with the recent release of declassified election-related intelligence, it's worth taking a closer look. This second installment from the Election Oversight Group compares documented election incidents with vulnerabilities described in the released intelligence, examining questions around election systems, chain of custody, auditability, and unauthorized access. Just days after a criminal referral involving Fulton County's 2020 election, the FBI sent a letter requesting election records—including ballots, tally sheets, and poll tapes. The document has reignited questions about how the investigation was handled and why transparency remains essential. At long last, in many ways, from many directions, here comes the sun.

Read the Post

The Nation Has Spoken

New Gallup: 73% of Americans are concerned about how the 2026 elections will be run.

Nearly three in four Americans.

Confidence cannot be mandated. It must be earned through transparency, accountability, and a system worthy of the public's trust.

Read More

Lead from Where You Stand

You can check your own voter registration record right now. Visit truethevote.org/registration and take three minutes to:

  1. Confirm your current record is accurate — your name, address, and status.
  2. Check the rolls in states where you used to live — old registrations often linger for years after you've moved, sometimes without your knowledge.
  3. Tell us what you found. Good or bad, we want to hear from you — and if something looks off, we're here to help you fix it.

Tools for Your Toolkit

You weren't meant to do this alone. Find your community, your tools, your purpose.

Become a Member

True the Vote will keep doing our part. With faith as our foundation and patriots like you standing in the gap, we'll keep pressing for transparency, accountability, and an America we leave stronger than we found it.

Grounded in Truth

Father, Thank You for giving us the unchanging truth of Your Word in a world filled with constantly changing opinions and messages. When the world tells us to follow our hearts, teach us to follow You. When the world labels us by our past, remind us that we are new creations in Christ. item.title: Less Than 60 Days
item.description:
| Read Online​

​

Idaho did it in 31. Here's how.

​

Hi Friend,

People love to say government moves slowly, and while it often does, legislation can be the exception.

Sometimes a bill is introduced, debated, amended, passed by both chambers, signed by the governor, and already changing how your elections are run - all before most Americans have heard a word about it.

Following these cycles and understanding the patterns prepares you for the next season. Check out these three very different bills in three states, and then see what may have passed in less than 60 days yours. Understanding these patterns will better prepare you for the next session cycle.

Highlights:

  • South Dakota now requires the Secretary of State to post the entire statewide voter file online every Monday. Introduced to signed: 55 days.
  • Utah banned wireless-capable voting equipment and handed equipment selection to the Lieutenant Governor, with a hard deadline already ticking. 46 days.
  • Idaho set a new 120-night residency test for legislative candidates, and the legal questions started before the ink dried. 31 days.

​South Dakota SB 214: 55 days

February 3 - March 30, 2026

It started as a simple idea: require the Secretary of State to publish South Dakota's complete statewide voter registration file online, every single Monday. Then it started moving.

The Senate committee passed it 9–0 on February 9. The full Senate followed the next day, 34–0. The House committee amended it and sent it through 11–1 on February 25, and the House floor cleared it 36–30 on March 3 (the one genuinely contested vote in the whole run). The Senate agreed to the House changes 34–0 on March 5. On March 30, Governor Larry Rhoden signed it into law.

Signing it was the starting gun. The Secretary of State now carries a brand new statutory duty: post the full statewide voter file online every Monday from now on. An entirely new administrative machine was built in under two months.

​Utah HB 26: 46 days

January 20 - March 7, 2026

Utah overhauled how voting equipment gets picked and certified in one bill. HB 26 bans wireless-capable voting equipment outright, repeals certification for ranked-choice voting equipment, and moves equipment selection to the Lieutenant Governor. 46 days from introduction to Governor Spencer Cox's signature.

The law immediately put the Lieutenant Governor's office on the hook: appoint a new Voting Equipment Selection Committee, run a competitive procurement process, open a public comment period, and certify equipment under the new wireless-ban standard - all against a hard lock-in date of May 6, 2026.

​Idaho H 810: 31 days

March 2 - April 2, 2026

This one moved even faster. H 810 sets a new residency test for legislative candidates: 120 nights of physical presence before filing, with exemptions only for active military and religious missions.

Unlike the others, the floor fights were real. 42–26, then 20–14, then 38–28. It still passed both chambers and reached Governor Brad Little's desk in 31 days. No lawsuit has been filed, but the legal conversation has already started: the analysts at Codify Legal Publishing note that the mismatched residency windows "raise equal-protection and ballot-access questions that courts could be asked to resolve." The law doesn't take effect until January 1, 2027, so the questions are live even though no case is. No agency guidance has been issued yet.

Before the ice could thaw...

...South Dakota had a new administrative machine, Utah had a new committee, and Idaho had a new residency requirement on the books.

The legislative process isn't measured in years. Sometimes it's measured in days. Today's committee agenda becomes tomorrow's election procedure. But that speed cuts both ways. The same process that pushes a bill through in 31 days is one you can use too - and the quiet weeks between sessions are exactly when that work gets done.

Now that you've seen how fast this moves, stay tuned. Next week, we'll show you how to build your own model legislation between sessions so you're ready before the gavel drops.

item.title: Where do we even start..?
item.description:
Let's Do This. Together.

​

Hi Friend,

Of all the questions we hear, this is the one that comes up most: "I want to help. Where do I start?"

Today's TTVN Live answered it, and the answer might surprise you.

Most people assume working at the polls begins on Election Day, but it doesn't. And that's actually good news, because it means there's still time. There's still time for you.

Newsletter highlights:

  • The #1 question we hear — "I want to help. Where do I start?"
  • Catherine's counterintuitive tip: serve inside the process before you ever try to investigate it (it's how TTV began)
  • A role-by-role breakdown from the easiest entry point to the ones needing training, plus exactly how to get plugged in
  • The training truth most people miss: guidance courses ≠ the certification your county requires

What if you've never worked in an election?

Don't worry about becoming an expert overnight. You just have to begin.

As Catherine put it on yesterday's TTVN Live episode, now is the season to find where you fit.

She ran through the various roles: poll workers, poll observers, precinct volunteers, citizen researchers, legislative advocates, public records investigators, voter registration teams, community educators — there isn't one way to serve. There are dozens. The only wrong move is waiting until Election Day to start.

Here's the part that catches people off guard...

Our strongest advice is to volunteer inside the election process before you ever try to investigate it.

Master tip...this is how Catherine was inspired to start TTV!

Work a polling location, observe an election, and watch how check-in works and how ballots actually move.

Once you've seen how elections really function, everything else clicks into place as your research gets stronger, your questions get sharper, and your conclusions get more accurate. Context is everything.

Did you know there are a variety of positions?

Here's the lay of the land, from easiest entry point to the ones that need a little more training:

  • Poll Watcher/Observer (also called poll challenger, depending on your state) — The best place to start if you've never done this before. You work on behalf of a party or candidate and simply observe the process. You don't talk to voters; if you see something, you report it to the judge running the polling place. Watch, take notes, learn how it all works.
  • Election Worker (behind the desk) — The most-needed role, because the polls can't function without it. You work for the county during the election period as a paid contract worker, checking registrations and getting voters their ballots. The goal is parity of party at the polls: equal Republican and Democrat representation. In many places, the Republican side is short-staffed, and both parties need to be present to make this work.
  • Mail Ballot Review Board — Review incoming absentee ballots and verify the signatures on security envelopes. (Some states have shifted this to automated AI review, so availability varies.)
  • Central Count Worker — Serve at the collection points where ballots are returned and tallied after the polls close. We all remember how 2020 looked in those counting rooms; this is where citizen eyes are essential.
  • Deputy Voter Registrar — Get certified to register voters in your community. (We'll dedicate a whole podcast to this one soon!)

How to get plugged in: Go to Engage → Toolkits or → Info by State on our website. Pick your state, use the Party Info link to connect directly with the party of your choice, and check the Election Info tab for your local "become a poll worker" link. You can also call your county or your local party or candidate directly and ask, "I want to serve, what are my options?"

One thing the online forms can't replace: at some point you'll need to talk to a real person to get on the calendar and assigned. And you'll almost always need to complete a training first.

​

Sign Up to Receive Volunteer Newsletters

​

And an important note: Organizations like True the Vote, establishment and party groups, and other well-meaning volunteers will provide training for guidance purposes. These important courses are generally the "how-to's" and "what if's" for working at the polls (especially if you don't know where to start!), but they do not replace the certification process that is almost always required.

I cannot tell you how many disheartened emails we receive on Election Day from citizens who were led to believe they sat through a course and felt prepared to work the polls, only to be told that they never properly registered, took the class, and got certified through their county.

Always make sure you check with your local elections office to confirm you take the required course(s) to be properly trained up and certified.

The time you put in early counts more than we can express.

We say it often at True the Vote: safeguarding elections was never meant to rest on a handful of "experts". It rests on an engaged citizenry.

Some volunteers spend hours on research. Some file open records requests or track legislation. Some work the polls, and some pray. Some simply nudge a neighbor to get involved.

Every one of those roles counts, because confidence in our elections isn't built by one organization, and it certainly is not built by the parties. It's built by citizens who choose to participate.

So if you've been waiting for the right moment to start, this is it. And there's still time!

Let's get to work.

item.title: Doors Are Opening. Enter the antagonists.
item.description:
| Read Online​

From Catherine

Hi Friend —

Something is different this week. You can feel the shift.

For years we said the same thing to the same closed doors. Our elections are riddled with process problems, which make them vulnerable to fraud. The records will show it, if anyone will only look. And for years the answer came back as a shrug, empty promises, hollow press releases, another door closing.

This week, doors are opening. Let's start with the rolls, because that is where all of this started for True the Vote back in the day.

Twenty-five states are now running sixty-eight million registrations through the SAVE database, flagging more than 480,000 questionable records in just ten states, so the numbers will continue to climb. And that is from a fairly narrow look. The real number of bad records, if ever exposed through a comprehensive audit, would be exponentially higher. But it is a good start.

Enter the antagonists. Four states — California, New Jersey, Nevada, Pennsylvania — refuse to run a SAVE check at all. Homeland Security estimates over 250,000 noncitizen registrations would be found sitting on their rolls. Of course, those four states say the DHS numbers can't be trusted.

Then, on July 21, the Governor of New Jersey reluctantly admitted that 6,600 noncitizens had been added to the state's rolls and that four hundred of them had voted — but insisted it was a software glitch. The company that wrote the software says her state's own process approved them, and based on our information, we side with the vendor. The process itself is what's broken. The software just digitized it.

The argument at the center of this debacle is the reliability of the SAVE database. SAVE was originally designed to check eligibility for social service benefits, not for voting. But it does contain data useful in determining citizenship status, which is what informs voting eligibility.

So we are told that SAVE sometimes returns a bad match, and therefore all checking should stop. Think of it. What business closes its books because the ledger didn't balance on the first pass? A flagged record is a question, not a verdict. To refuse to look is not caution. It is a way of choosing not to know. Cleaning up the rolls is bookkeeping. It is not a millstone to hang around a voter's neck, and it is not — for crying out loud — a scheme to keep anyone from voting. Either a person qualifies to vote or they don't.

Which brings us to a reality check, because the real work, if it is to be done, can’t start in databases at all. It has to start in us. In two years, confidence that our elections are run fairly and accurately has fallen off a cliff, from 76% down to 66% nationwide. And 83% of us want voter ID. Americans want common sense reforms.

And it's not about just citizenship checks, or ID, or basic record accuracy, or mail ballots, or month long voting, or machines, or foreign influence, its about all of it.

Confidence in elections will not be won back by political arguments. It will be won back by good housekeeping and practical improvements in our processes. The reason politicians can't make this a pitch for common sense is that they are conditioned to saber-rattling. item.title: The Domino Effect
item.description:
| Read Online​

​

One law. One court case. Then everything changes.

​

Hi Friend,

The first domino never looks like much.

A single sentence, tucked inside a single section of a single law. No headlines or fanfare. Just a quiet decision that decades later almost no one remembers being made. But it leans against the next one, and the next, and by the time anyone notices, the whole row is falling.

History rarely changes overnight. It changes when one decision quietly sets a hundred others in motion: a law passed, a lawsuit filed, a ruling handed down, a rule rewritten by an agency almost no one is watching. Years later, plenty of people remember the controversy, but hardly anyone remembers the first domino that started it.

And here's the part that should make all of us pay attention: that first domino almost always begins with a good intention.

A domino that reshaped the country:

Picture Washington in 1965. Congress passes the Voting Rights Act, a landmark law meant to stop racial discrimination at the ballot box. One provision does the heavy lifting: Section 5. It says certain states and jurisdictions with a history of discrimination can't change any election law until the federal government signs off first. They called it "preclearance." Ask permission, then act. For nearly fifty years, that's how it worked.

Then a second domino tipped, and this is where we see the most frustration.

In 2013, the Supreme Court decided Shelby County v. Holder. The Court didn't strike down preclearance itself, but rather the formula used to decide who was covered, ruling that it was built on decades-old data. Congress could have written a new formula, but never did. And just like that, states that had spent half a century asking permission could now change their election laws without asking anyone.

Whether you see this as restoring state sovereignty or removing a federal safeguard, one thing is beyond dispute: a single ruling redrew election law across the entire country. That one domino set off years of new bills, lawsuits, constitutional fights, and policy shifts, and they're still falling today.

The domino falling right now (and you're familiar with it):

We're watching another first domino tip as we speak - one you're already familiar with: the SAVE Act. Whether or not it ultimately passes, it's already having a catalyzing effect in state legislatures across the country.

Lawmakers all over are filing bills requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote. Mississippi's SHIELD Act is already law and in effect. And right now, in three different states, three more dominoes are mid-fall, and each one leaning toward a different downstream fight.

  1. ​Arizona HCR 2001: The "Fast Election Results Act" isn't just another bill. It's a constitutional amendment demanding citizens-only voting, proof of citizenship, and voter ID. The legislature already passed it and sent it to the Secretary of State on June 15 for the ballot. It's the same species as Mississippi's SHIELD Act, but with higher stakes, because voters themselves will decide it. Its passage sets up exactly the kind of post-election court fight that Shelby County became, and the sort of ruling that could reshape how Arizona verifies eligibility for years.
  2. ​Delaware HB 317: The domino leans a different direction. HB 317 would order the DMV to audit automatic voter registrations tied to documents that aren't REAL-ID compliant. Look closely and you'll see the same fault line running under it that runs under the SAVE fight: it lives or dies on cross-checking ID and citizenship records against each other, the precise kind of database-verification dispute already drawing conflicting federal rulings elsewhere.
  3. ​New Hampshire HB 1062: The quietest of the three, and would let the Secretary of State randomly audit registered voters' citizenship claims and refer suspected noncitizens to the attorney general; it sits in conference committee as of late May. It's the narrow, audit-based cousin of the citizenship wave, and its data-sharing and referral provisions make it a prime candidate for the due-process and privacy lawsuits that tend to trail every eligibility-verification program ever built.

Three states. Three dominoes. One tips toward the ballot box, one toward a database, one toward the courthouse — and caught in the middle are the people who actually run your elections, county clerks and registrars left guessing which rule applies this week.

​

Here's the piece most people miss. All of this rests on a rule we treat as bedrock: you have to be a citizen to vote. Federally, that's 18 U.S.C. § 611 which states that it's a crime for a noncitizen to vote in a federal election. Sounds airtight. But read one section further, to § 611(c), and there's a built-in exception: no prosecution if the person's parents were citizens, they lived here since before age 16, and they "reasonably believed … that he or she was a citizen." The federal backstop has a door in it. That's exactly why these three dominoes aren't random — they're states verifying citizenship up front, at registration, to close a gap federal law leaves open.

The National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) of 1993 ... sets forth guidelines for voter registration in federal elections, including documentation requirements and the ability for states to use mail-in and agency-based
registration processes. While it did not address the need for documentary proof of citizenship (DPOC), it mandates attestation under penalty of perjury for voter eligibility, limiting states’ ability to impose DPOC requirements for federal elections.
- Excerpt from True the Vote's "The 611 Project"​

The thing about a first domino is that it never stays put. One bill becomes a burden on the clerk down the road. One court order becomes an appeal, then an amendment, then the template for the next state's bill. The row keeps falling quietly and steadily whether or not anyone is watching.

As Americans, we hold the keys to our government, but a key only works if we turn it. Legislative tracking looks intimidating at first, but it comes down to one thing: seeing how a single decision in law sets off the chain that shapes who controls our elections today. Understand the chain, spot the holes, and we can help close them.

So the only real question is: who's watching the first domino?

You are. The citizen willing to do the almost-forgotten work of paying attention before a law is a headline. That's the whole point of LegiTrack: we follow these bills from the moment they're filed, because by the time a change is famous, the domino has already fallen.

Identify the first one, and you can catch it before the rest fall.

Ever onward -

Help Us Stay in the Fight

Truth Social: @LegiTrack | X: @Real_LegiTrack​

​

The Cost of Unequal Enforcement

​

Hi Friend,

At True the Vote, one of our core missions is education which often means taking a step back to understand the events that brought us here. History provides context, legislation creates the framework, and court decisions establish precedent. By understanding how yesterday shaped today, we can better appreciate how the decisions being made today will shape tomorrow.

Some background

In 2013, Congress held hearings into something most Americans never imagined possible: a federal agency admitting it had singled out organizations because of their names and beliefs.

The Internal Revenue Service acknowledged that when certain groups applied for tax-exempt status, it had flagged them based on what they were called and what they stood for—not on anything they had actually done:

Independent Sector is deeply troubled that applications for tax exempt status were singled out by IRS personnel for additional scrutiny based on the applying organizations’ names or the nature of their exempt activities. The IRS’s proper role in approving, and subsequently regulating, exempt organizations is not determining the worthiness of their cause, but their compliance with the law.

After years of harassment, unequal treatment, fines, and government investigations that extended beyond the scope of their tax-exempt applications, the organizations under scrutiny could have given up. The easier path would have been to throw up their hands, say, "Forget it," and walk away.

But they didn't.

Catherine was amongst the group of citizens who chose to do the hard thing: fight.

​

Regardless of political affiliation, one principle should unite Americans:

Government agencies should apply the law—not political preferences.

Here's what happened, how this applies today within LegiTrack, and which bills we're tracking this week.

In case you missed it:

For roughly 18 months beginning in 2010, employees in the IRS Determinations Unit flagged applications for tax-exempt status using keywords like "Tea Party," "Patriots," and "9/12"—later expanding to groups focused on government spending, debt, taxes, and the Constitution. What surfaced at the 2013 hearings was straightforward:

  • The IRS acknowledged that its screening had been inappropriate.
  • The Inspector General confirmed the criteria were improper—based on names and beliefs, not activities.
  • Some organizations waited nearly three years for a decision, and dozens faced improper requests for information like donor lists.
  • Congress spent months investigating how it happened and who knew.
  • And Americans across the spectrum asked one question: "Can government be trusted to treat everyone equally?"

So why revisit a hearing from more than a decade ago?

Because the question never changed. While the agency may be different, the issue isn't.

When oversight becomes precedent...

The IRS controversy didn't end when the hearings adjourned. What Congress exposed, the courts took up—years of litigation, rulings, and settlements that reinforced longstanding constitutional protections: the First Amendment rights to free speech and association, and the principle that government cannot selectively burden citizens for their political views.

Court decisions don't just settle a single dispute—they become part of the framework that guides future conduct. Agencies weigh those rulings when writing policy, legislators draft with those guardrails in mind, and citizens gain clearer standards for challenging overreach.

Oversight revealed the problem. The courts helped establish the principles that make similar conduct harder to justify. It's a reminder that legislation, oversight, and the judiciary each play a distinct but essential role in preserving constitutional government—today's bills become tomorrow's laws, and those laws may one day be tested in court, shaping the precedents that protect future generations.

The same principle applies to elections:

This is where LegiTrack comes in.

Election officials wield enormous authority over voter rolls, ballots, investigations, certification, and public records. Whether those powers are exercised fairly—or even appear to be exercised fairly—determines public confidence.

The IRS story wasn't ultimately about tax forms. It was about whether a government body could be trusted to treat citizens the same regardless of their views. Elections raise the same test, just in a different arena. When a voter is added or removed from a roll, when a ballot is handled and stored, when a records request is answered or delayed, the question underneath is identical: is the law being applied evenly?

Trust is created by transparent laws that apply equally to everyone.

Every week, legislatures introduce, amend, and debate bills that determine how elections are administered. Some move quickly. Others remain active for months before becoming law—or becoming the subject of litigation.

​LegiTrack follows them throughout that process because the final vote isn't always the most important part of the story. Some expand or limit oversight, increase or reduce public confidence, or raise new questions entirely.

Here's what's on our radar (and a few you may have missed):

1. Federal — H.R. 9577, the "COCOA-VIP Act" (introduced July 1, 2026) · Observer access. Amends the Help America Vote Act to affirm congressional election observers' access to federal primary elections.

Watch: How Congress defines oversight—and who is entitled to observe federal elections.

2. New Jersey — S 4523 (Introduced June 25, 2026 but sitting) · Audits and citizenship verification. Requires the Secretary of State and Motor Vehicle Commission to audit voter registrations going forward, and requires proof of citizenship to register at the MVC.

Watch: How the state balances election security with standards for verifying voter eligibility. Right now is a great time to reach out to your state reps to be heard.

3. Michigan — SB 1087 (Introduced) · Money in elections. Would revoke the ability of limited liability companies to spend money supporting or opposing candidates, parties, committees, or ballot initiatives; such expenditures would be invalid and subject to legal action, including possible dissolution, with carve-outs for existing obligations and certain media activities. Tie-barred with SB 1085 and SB 1086, so it takes effect only if those pass.

Watch: Where lawmakers draw the line on political spending and who may participate in elections financially.

4. Federal — S 4774, the "FAIR Elections Act of 2026" (introduced June 10, 2026 and also sitting) · Voter-roll integrity. Amends voter registration law to bar removing names from the rolls based on unverified databases, and prohibits false AI-generated election media.

Watch: How the bill defines "reliable" voter-roll maintenance while limiting the use of certain data sources.

5. New York — S 10563 (First Chamber) · Ballot handling. Requires a notice on all mail-return ballots explaining timely return methods, including information on drop boxes.

Watch: How election officials communicate ballot return requirements and the role of voter education in ballot administration. Keep an eye out for language edits and curveballs as it progresses forward.

History rarely repeats itself in exactly the same way, but it often asks the same questions.

Should government operate transparently? Should laws be applied equally? Should citizens be able to verify what government is doing?

Those aren't partisan questions. They're constitutional ones.

We'll keep watching the legislation that helps answer them.

item.title: Tug of War
item.description:
​

Ten Bills, Two Directions

​

Hi Friend,

Congress and state legislatures have been busy.

The past few weeks brought a fresh wave of election bills pulling in two directions: some strengthening election safeguards, others making those safeguards harder to enact or defend. Together they'd reshape who can vote, how elections are audited, and how campaigns are funded.

Here's what we're watching.

Highlights

  • HR 9368 (Voter ID Act) is the one with momentum. Introduced June 17, marked up and ordered reported by House Administration just six days later. Photo ID for federal elections, with a free-ID grant program and provisional-ballot fallback.
  • HR 9264 would end non-citizen voting loopholes at the federal level — and make unlawful non-citizen voting grounds for inadmissibility or deportation. Referred to House Judiciary.
  • Georgia wants its voters to settle the citizenship question themselves. SR 4 would put a citizens-only voting amendment directly on the ballot for ratification.
  • North Carolina's SB 1087 would hand post-election audits to the State Auditor — not election officials — covering voter rolls, equipment, tabulation records, and absentee/provisional handling after every general election. Public reports required.
  • June 23 was the big day on the other side of the aisle. House and Senate Democrats introduced the "Right to Vote" pair (HR 9437 / S 4884) and a resolution (HRES 1384) calling for restored preclearance, a filibuster carve-out for voting bills, and Supreme Court ethics rules, term limits, and possible expansion — all on the same day.
  • Michigan is pulling in opposite directions. Senate Republicans filed SB 1054 to end no-reason absentee voting on June 23; Senate Democrats answered on July 2 with SB 1086 and companions to bar corporate and nonprofit election spending.

Top 5 Bills Strengthening Election Integrity (Newly Introduced)

US HR 9264 — No Exceptions for Non-Citizens Voting Act

  • Issue: Closes federal loopholes that currently let certain non-citizens vote, and makes unlawful non-citizen voting grounds for inadmissibility/deportation.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Ogles, Moore, Burlison (R)
  • Status: Introduced 6/10/26; referred to House Judiciary.

US HR 9368 — Voter ID Act

  • Issue: Amends the Help America Vote Act to require photo ID to vote in federal elections, with a free-ID grant program and provisional-ballot fallback.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Miller, Murphy, Hinson, Griffith, Steil, Carey, Lee, Kim (R)
  • Status: Introduced 6/17/26; marked up and ordered reported by House Administration, 6/23/26. Fastest mover on this list.

Georgia SR 4 — Citizens-Only Voting Amendment

  • Issue: Proposed constitutional amendment stating only U.S. citizens may vote in Georgia elections, to be ratified directly by voters.
  • Sponsors: Sens. Dolezal, Walker, Anavitarte, Still, and others (R)
  • Status: Filed 6/17/26; read and referred in the Senate.

North Carolina SB 1087 — Post-Election Audits by State Auditor

  • Issue: Requires the State Auditor to audit voter rolls, voting equipment, tabulation records, and absentee/provisional ballot handling in selected counties after every general election, with public reports.
  • Sponsors: Sens. Overcash, Daniel, Hise (R)
  • Status: Filed 6/17/26; passed 1st reading, referred to Rules.

Michigan SB 1054 — Eliminate No-Reason Absentee Voting

  • Issue: Would repeal Michigan's no-excuse absentee voting and require voters to cite disability, religious tenets, age, or absence from precinct to get an absentee ballot.
  • Sponsors: Sens. Lindsey, McBroom, Lauwers, Daley, Bellino (R)
  • Status: Introduced 6/23/26; referred to Committee on Elections and Ethics.

Top 5 Bills Reshaping Election Law (Newly Introduced)

US HR 9437 — Right to Vote Act

  • Issue: Would require any government action that burdens voting to survive strict "least restrictive means" judicial review — a standard critics say would expose voter-ID and citizenship-verification laws to nationwide court challenges.
  • Sponsors: Rep. Neguse and 25 others (D)
  • Status: Introduced 6/23/26; referred to House Judiciary.

US S 4884 — Senate Companion Protecting the Right to Vote

  • Issue: Senate counterpart addressing the same "undue burden" voting-rights framework.
  • Sponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Cantwell, Hickenlooper, Hirono, King, Klobuchar, Merkley, Padilla, and others (D)
  • Status: Introduced 6/23/26; referred to Rules and Administration.

US HRES 1384 — Sense of the House Resolution

  • Issue: Non-binding resolution calling for restoring Voting Rights Act preclearance, eliminating the Senate filibuster to pass voting legislation, and imposing a Supreme Court ethics code, term limits, and possible Court expansion.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Clarke, Espaillat, Meng, Johnson, Casar, Mfume (D)
  • Status: Submitted 6/23/26; referred to House Judiciary.

Michigan SB 1086 (companion bills SB 1085, SB 1087 — not to be confused with North Carolina's SB 1087 above)

  • Issue: Would revoke the power of nonprofit corporations, business corporations, and LLCs to spend money on elections or ballot issues.
  • Sponsors: Sens. McCann, Hertel, Irwin, Cherry, Chang, Bayer, Cavanagh, Shink, +1 (D)
  • Status: Introduced 7/2/26; referred to Committee on Elections and Ethics.

And on a bonus note: DOJ just sent Michigan a letter reminding election officials that federal law requires clean voter rolls — and that keeping ineligible names on the list can carry criminal penalties.

US HR 9354 — Fair Elections Now Act

  • Issue: Creates a taxpayer-funded "Fair Elections Fund" that matches small-dollar House campaign donations, with a new federal board regulating candidate eligibility and debate participation.
  • Sponsor: Rep. Larson (D)
  • Status: Introduced 6/17/26; referred to House Administration.

Why We're Watching

This batch signals two competing destinations for election law: one path adds verification, audits, and ID requirements state by state, while the other builds federal authority over how those laws get written, funded, and challenged in court. HR 9368 already cleared its first committee hurdle in under a week, so this fight is moving faster than most.

It's pretty clear this legislative tug of war has ramped up. We'll keep tracking every one of these on LegiTrack so the headlines never catch you off guard.

How to Volunteer at True the Vote

​

​

Hi Friend,

One of the questions we hear most often is:

"I'd love to help...but where do I start?"

Whether you're passionate about learning, research, technology, legislation, community building, or hands-on action, True the Vote offers meaningful ways to put your skills and interests to work.

You don't need endless free time to make a difference. Five minutes a week or several hours a day can have an impact, and there is a place for you.

Here's where to begin.

Tip: if you're a part of the TTVN Community, click on an action item to take you directly to your preferred Space!

Join TTVN for Free

Knowledge comes first.

Before taking action, understand how elections actually work, and test your own knowledge! It's never too late to brush up.

  • Lessons
  • Quizzes
  • Constitution series
  • Election process education
  • Weekly newsletters
  • TTVN Live

"An informed citizen is an effective citizen."

No one should have to fight alone.

Inside TTVN you'll find:

  • State groups
  • Local discussions

5. Help Your Community

Once you're comfortable...

  • Invite people into TTVN

Every informed citizen strengthens another.

One of our fastest-growing efforts.

Learn how to:

  • Submit Open Records Requests

  • Read reports
